strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open problem: no prior work achieves Best-of-Both-Worlds (BoBW) guarantees for episodic MDPs with heavy-tailed feedback in both known- and unknown-transition settings; this paper provides the first such results.

Solid and detailed technical contributions: a novel skipping loss estimator adapted to occupancy measures, a new local-control analysis for heavy-tailed shifted losses (pointwise and second-moment bounds), and a suboptimal mass propagation lemma that generalizes the MAB 'exclude optimal action' trick to the occupancy-measure polytope.

For unknown transitions, the paper introduces a pessimistic skipping-loss estimator combined with Upper Occupancy Bounds and a four-term regret decomposition (transition/estimation/skipping/pessimism error) that cleanly isolates heavy-tailed estimation error from transition uncertainty; this is a nontrivial and instructive contribution technically.

The derived rates recover/match existing results as special cases: reduces to the tight heavy-tailed MAB bounds of Bubeck et al. (2013) and to Jin & Luo (2020)/Jin et al. (2021) bounds when α=2, providing sanity checks on correctness and tightness with respect to T and gap parameters.
The paper is thorough in its proofs (extensive appendix with careful lemma-by-lemma derivations), which supports reproducibility of the theoretical results in principle.
weaknesses: No empirical validation whatsoever; the paper is purely theoretical with no experiments or even toy simulations to sanity-check the algorithms or illustrate practical behavior of the skipping/pessimism mechanisms.

The regret bounds have very poor (and seemingly not carefully optimized) polynomial dependence on H, S, A (e.g., terms like H^{α+1}S^{2-2/α}A^{4-4/α}, or H^{α^2/(α-1)+1}S^2A^4 in the unknown-transition self-bounding case), which the authors themselves flag as future work; this substantially limits the practical significance of the results even if the T-dependence is tight.

The algorithms require knowledge of tail parameters (σ, α) to set constants C, β, D precisely (Eqs. 16-17), unlike some recent 'parameter-free' heavy-tailed bandit BoBW works cited in related work (e.g., Chen et al. 2025); the lack of parameter-free adaptivity is a notable limitation not fully discussed.

The self-bounding regret bound for the unknown-transition case (Theorem 5.1/C.1) is very complex with many additive terms and multiple auxiliary quantities (ω∆(2), ω∆(α), ∆min, Csb-dependent terms), making it hard to assess overall tightness or to compare cleanly against natural lower bounds beyond the adversarial regime.

Presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy even in the main text; core intuitions (e.g., why local control of shifted losses is needed, why suboptimal mass propagation works) are described somewhat tersely, requiring heavy reliance on the appendix to follow the argument.

The paper does not discuss computational complexity/tractability of solving the FTRL optimization over Q(P) or Q(hat P_i) with the 1/α-Tsallis regularizer in practice, nor the practical cost of the Comp-UOB procedure repeated every episode.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely open and well-motivated problem: achieving Best-of-Both-Worlds (BoBW) guarantees for episodic MDPs under heavy-tailed feedback, bridging two previously separate lines of work (BoBW MDPs with bounded losses and heavy-tailed MDPs restricted to stochastic environments).

The technical contributions are substantial and non-trivial: the paper introduces a novel skipping loss estimator embedded into FTRL over occupancy measures with a 1/alpha-Tsallis entropy regularizer, a local control technique for bounding pointwise and second-moment properties of heavy-tailed shifted losses (Lemmas 4.2/4.3), and a suboptimal mass propagation lemma (Lemma 4.4) that generalizes the MAB-style 'exclude the optimal action' argument to the occupancy-measure setting of MDPs.

The extension to unknown transitions (HT-FTRL-UOB) is a meaningful further contribution, introducing a pessimistic estimator combined with Upper Occupancy Bounds and a four-way regret decomposition (transition error, estimation error, skipping error, pessimism error) that cleanly isolates the heavy-tailed-specific difficulties from the standard UOB machinery.

The results are shown to recover or match known special cases: reduction to MAB lower bounds (Bubeck et al. 2013) in tightness with respect to sigma, T, and gaps, and recovery of Jin & Luo (2020)/Jin et al. (2021) bounds when alpha=2, lending credibility to the correctness and tightness of the bounds.

The paper is exceptionally thorough in its proofs; appendices provide detailed, mostly self-contained derivations of all key lemmas (loss shifting, stability, penalty, skipping error bounds) which supports reproducibility of the theoretical results.
The related work section is comprehensive and carefully situates the contribution relative to heavy-tailed bandits, heavy-tailed MDPs, and BoBW MDP literature, clarifying what is genuinely novel.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation (simulations or experiments) to illustrate the practical behavior of the proposed algorithms or to sanity-check the theoretical rates, which would strengthen confidence in the results and their practical relevance.

The polynomial dependence on H, S, A in the regret bounds appears quite large (e.g., terms scaling like H^{alpha+1}, S^{2-2/alpha}A^{4-4/alpha} or worse in the self-bounding regime with unknown transitions), and the paper itself acknowledges tightening these factors as future work; the current dependence may limit practical significance even though the T-dependence is near-optimal.

The self-bounding regret bound for the unknown-transition case (Theorem 5.1) is comparatively complex and the paper does not provide much intuition or a clean simplified statement helping readers see the dominant terms in typical regimes, making it harder to judge practical implications from the theorem alone.

The paper assumes knowledge of the heavy-tail parameters (alpha, sigma) in the algorithm design (e.g., in setting C, beta, D), and while this is consistent with much of the heavy-tailed bandit/RL literature, related work (e.g., Chen et al. 2025 on parameter-free heavy-tailed MABs) suggests parameter-free extensions are of interest but are not discussed as a limitation or addressed here.

Some of the technical machinery (e.g., loss shifting, self-bounding decomposition, UOB) is adapted relatively directly from Jin et al. (2021) and Huang et al. (2022)/Zhao et al. (2025), so while the combination and heavy-tailed-specific extensions (shifted loss control, suboptimal mass propagation, pessimistic estimator) are novel, a reader familiar with these prior works may view part of the contribution as an application of known techniques to a new setting rather than a conceptually new set of tools.
